text: Okay, is this thing recording? Alright. So, the dal. Your grandmother always made the dal on Sundays, and everybody asks me how, so here it is. You take, oh, about one cup of the yellow lentils, the toor dal, and you wash it, three, four times, until the water is clear. Then into the pressure cooker with maybe three cups of water, a pinch of turmeric, and some salt. Four whistles. Four, not three, she was very strict about that. Meanwhile, in a small pan, you heat two spoons of ghee. Real ghee, not that oil business. When it is hot you put one teaspoon of cumin seeds, and they will splutter, then two dried red chillies, and a big pinch of hing, the asafoetida. Then one onion chopped fine, and you let it go golden. Then one tomato, and two cloves of garlic, crushed. Cook it till the tomato is soft and mushy. Then you pour this whole thing, the tadka, into the dal and mix. Squeeze half a lemon. Fresh coriander on top. This is enough for four people, or for two if I am eating. You know, we made this the day your father was born, the whole hospital floor could smell it. Anyway. That is the dal.

Right, banana bread. This one I learned from Mrs. Fernandes next door, back in, what, nineteen seventy eight? She would never write anything down either. So. You want three bananas, very ripe, the ugly black ones that nobody wants to eat. Mash them up with a fork in a big bowl. Then half a cup of butter, melted, a stick, pour that in. Three quarters of a cup of sugar, I use brown sugar, she used white, it does not matter much. One egg, beaten. A teaspoon of vanilla. Then you put in one teaspoon of baking soda and a pinch of salt, and then one and a half cups of flour, the plain flour. Do not over mix it, just until the flour disappears, otherwise it gets tough, like a brick. Oh, and if you have walnuts, a handful of walnuts, chopped. Grease a loaf tin, pour it in, and bake at, three fifty Fahrenheit, about one hundred and seventy five Celsius, for about an hour. Poke it with a toothpick, if it comes out clean, it is done. Let it cool before you cut it, I know you won't, nobody does. Makes one loaf. Mrs. Fernandes used to bring it over every Christmas, wrapped in newspaper, still warm.

Ah, the chai. People think chai is just tea bags, no no no. Listen. For two cups, you put one cup of water and one cup of milk in a saucepan. Before it boils, you crush, in the mortar, about four green cardamom pods, a small piece of ginger, about one inch, and two cloves. And a little cinnamon if you like it, I like it. Throw all that into the water and milk and let it come to a boil. Then two teaspoons of loose black tea, the strong Assam kind. And two teaspoons of sugar, or more, your grandmother took three. Let it boil up, it will rise, and when it rises, you take it off the flame, let it settle, and put it back. Do this three times. This is the secret, three times. Then strain it into the cups. I drank this every morning at the railway station for forty years before work, the chaiwala there, Ramu, he taught me the three times trick.
